title: Impact of indoor environmental quality on occupant well-being and comfort: A review of the literature
review_question: To document the state of the art literature and analyse the key threads of thought regarding health and well-being of occupants of office buildings, and to establish links between IEQ parameters, health and well-being of occupants and implementation of green practices in building design.
inclusion_exclusion_criteria: Literature published between 1970 and 2015 (major focus 2000 onwards), including refereed journals, refereed conference proceedings, reports, and books. Selection based on journal reputation and citation count (top 10 cited papers highlighted). Focus on commercial and office buildings.

findings.antecedent: Indoor environmental quality (IEQ)
findings.quote: IEQ and its effect on occupant well-being and comfort is an important area of study.

findings.antecedent: Indoor environment (thermal, acoustic, visual, air quality)
findings.quote: Research has clearly established that problems with indoor environmental quality (IEQ) (thermal, acoustic, visual and air quality) of a building has a direct effect on the comfort, health and productivity of the occupants

findings.antecedent: Indoor air quality (IAQ)
findings.source: 3. Indoor air quality in office buildings
findings.quote: Indoor air quality (IAQ) is an important issue that has both short term and long term impacts on the health of occupants

findings.antecedent: Increased ventilation rate
findings.consequent: Indoor air quality (reduced air pollutant concentration)
findings.source: 3. Indoor air quality in office buildings
findings.quote: The first one is to improve the indoor air quality by increasing the ventilation rate, which in turn reduces air pollutant

findings.antecedent: Reduced source of pollution within and outside building
findings.source: 3. Indoor air quality in office buildings
findings.quote: The second is by reducing the source of pollution within and outside the building in order to reduce the introduction of pollutants in the indoor air.

findings.antecedent: Increased outdoor air supply rates in non-industrial environments
findings.consequent: Air quality and reduced concentration of air pollutants
findings.source: 3. Indoor air quality in office buildings
findings.quote: Recent studies have established that the increasing outdoor air supply rates in non-industrial environments improve the air quality and reduce the concentration of air pollutants

findings.antecedent: Properly designed natural ventilation system
findings.source: 3. Indoor air quality in office buildings
findings.quote: A properly designed natural ventilation system, if designed properly has the potential to provide considerable energy savings from cooling needs

findings.antecedent: Occupants of naturally ventilated offices
findings.source: 3. Indoor air quality in office buildings

findings.antecedent: Natural ventilation in cities with high outdoor air pollution (Particulate Matter, ozone)

findings.antecedent: Low polluting building material
findings.source: 3. Indoor air quality in office buildings
findings.quote: The new green building guidelines have focused on use of low polluting building material as well as effective management of IAQ through appropriate air handling systems

findings.antecedent: Indoor environment (office building or dwelling)

findings.antecedent: New construction material (not properly tested/certified), type of furniture, office equipment

findings.antecedent: Sick building syndrome (SBS)
findings.consequent: Self-reported illness absences and reduced productivity in offices
findings.quote: SBS leads to an increase in self-reported illness absences and reduced productivity in offices

findings.antecedent: Mechanically ventilated and air conditioned buildings
findings.consequent: Hospital visits (especially for female occupants) due to SBS
findings.quote: SBS leads to a rise in hospital visits especially for female occupants of mechanically ventilated and air conditioned buildings compared to occupants of naturally ventilated buildings

findings.antecedent: Moulds, dust, mite, allergens, indoor aldehydes, Volatile Organic Compounds (VOC), airborne fungi, pesticides, tobacco smoke, lighting, air exchange or circulation rates, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide
findings.quote: In addition to ventilation there are factors such as moulds, dust, mite, allergens, indoor aldehydes, Volatile Organic Compounds (VOC), airborne fungi, pesticides, tobacco smoke, lighting, air exchange or circulation rates, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide which may lead to SBS symptoms

findings.antecedent: Chronic exposure to air in water-damaged buildings
findings.consequent: Allergic and irritation symptoms on pulmonary functions
findings.quote: chronic exposure to the air in water-damaged buildings is often linked to allergic and irritation symptoms on pulmonary functions.

findings.antecedent: Fungal concentrations in floor or chair dust
findings.consequent: Eye irritation, asthma, upper respiratory symptoms, lower job satisfaction
findings.quote: fungal concentrations in floor or chair dust lead to eye irritation, asthma and upper respiratory symptoms

findings.antecedent: Building design that reduces exposure to indoor chemicals, continuous monitoring of indoor air, monitoring/control of water pipes/wet areas, appropriate third party certified building materials
findings.consequent: Good indoor environmental quality (IEQ) and reduction in SBS
findings.quote: it is important that buildings be designed that reduce the exposure to indoor chemicals, there should be a continuous monitoring of indoor air, as well as monitoring and control of all the water pipes and wet areas to avoid water leakage. Monitoring of water pipes will lead to reduction in dampness which is the root cause of lots of mould and mite related problems (Redd, 2002). Selection of appropriate, third party certified building materials is also crucial to ensure good indoor environmental quality [IEQ] and reduction in SBS

findings.antecedent: Thermal comfort

findings.antecedent: Occupant discomfort (thermal)
findings.consequent: Energy consumption (tweaking controls to non-optimal levels)

findings.antecedent: Six factors (air temperature, mean radiant temperature, air relative humidity, air velocity, metabolic rates, clothing insulation)
findings.quote: Thermal comfort is influenced by six factors; four of which that could be classified as environmental parameters include air temperature, mean radiant temperature, air relative humidity, and air velocity. The other two are classified as personal factors and include human metabolic rates and insulation through clothing

findings.antecedent: Building design phase consideration of thermal comfort factors
findings.quote: All these factors need to be considered at the design phase of the building itself

findings.antecedent: Gender, age, climatic conditions, location, typology of building, outdoor climate, season
findings.quote: Gender, age, and climatic conditions all have an impact on the thermal comfort perceived by the occupant... The location and typology of the building along with outdoor climate and season also influence thermal comfort of occupants

findings.antecedent: Passive design in buildings (especially in tropical climates)
findings.consequent: Optimal level of cooling and occupant comfort, less energy consumption
findings.quote: The concept of passive design in buildings has evolved over the last 15 years however, achieving passive standards in cold climate of Northern Europe is different from achieving it in Middle East where mechanical cooling is necessary to achieve optimal level of cooling and occupant comfort... Whereas, in tropical climate buildings are naturally ventilated and end up consuming significantly less energy, which gives occupants the feeling that they are closer to nature

findings.antecedent: Local air conditioning and task – ambient conditioning
findings.consequent: Well-maintained thermal comfort, less energy consumption
findings.quote: Thermal comfort is also found to be well-maintained using less energy consuming measures such as local air conditioning and task – ambient conditioning

findings.antecedent: Culture
findings.quote: The perception of comfort differs from one to the other climate and is also influenced by the culture

findings.antecedent: Behavioral adjustment, physiological adaptation, psychological habituation or expectation
findings.consequent: Thermal adaptation and perception of comfort
findings.quote: The eventual thermal adaptation of an occupant in an environment and their perception of comfort are defined by three factors: behavioural adjustment, physiological adaptation, and psychological habituation or expectation

findings.antecedent: Acoustic comfort

findings.antecedent: Open plan offices
findings.consequent: Acoustic comfort and privacy (issues impacting productivity)

findings.antecedent: Annoyance from various noises, lack of communication privacy

findings.antecedent: Noise from other people talking, telephones ringing, irregular sounds

findings.antecedent: Noise masking too loud

findings.antecedent: Visual comfort

findings.antecedent: Windows and natural views
findings.quote: Preference for windows and therapeutic impact of natural views is well established in the literature

findings.antecedent: Insufficient light and glare
findings.consequent: Ability to see objects or details clearly
findings.quote: Insufficient light and especially daylight or glare reduces the ability to see objects or details clearly

findings.antecedent: Architectural design (office lighting)
findings.quote: Architectural design has a direct impact on office lighting and office lighting has a direct impact on well-being and productivity.

findings.antecedent: Access to natural lighting and artificial lighting
findings.quote: The access to natural lighting as well as artificial lighting is essential in order to ensure well-being of occupants

findings.antecedent: Visual comfort at work
findings.consequent: Comfort after work and sleep quality at home
findings.quote: Visual comfort at work has an impact on comfort after work as well... There are studies that have looked at impact of visual comfort on sleep quality at home after work.

findings.antecedent: View type, view quality, social density
findings.consequent: Physical and psychological health of occupants
findings.quote: Several visual comfort criteria such as view type, view quality and social density have an impact on physical and psychological health of the occupants

findings.antecedent: Densely laid offices and open plan offices
findings.quote: Densely laid offices and open plan offices have negative effect on visual comfort which leads to a negative impact on occupant well-being

findings.antecedent: Geometry of windows, photometry of surfaces, amount of glazing
findings.consequent: Illumination levels in a work area
findings.quote: Geometry of windows, photometry of surfaces, amount of glazing etc., all have an impact on the illumination levels in a work area

findings.antecedent: Excessive use of artificial lighting
findings.consequent: Overall productivity, comfort, well-being of occupants
findings.quote: Visual comfort plays such a vital role in the overall productivity, comfort and well-being of the occupants that buildings need to avoid excessive use of artificial lighting yet still maintain some level of optimality

findings.antecedent: Energy efficiency (tighter building envelop, reduced ventilation rates)
findings.consequent: Occupant well-being (higher ventilation rate to dispel PM)

This is a conflict which is often decided in favour of building efficiency and not occupant well-being

findings.antecedent: Natural ventilation or higher rate of ventilation
findings.quote: For example natural ventilation or higher rate of ventilation may also have an adverse effect on acoustic comfort of occupants since it might allow more exterior background noise to come inside the building

findings.antecedent: Green buildings

findings.antecedent: Green building strategies (fewer barriers between noise sources and occupants)
findings.quote: Strategies in green buildings that provide fewer barriers between the sources of noises and occupants lead to poor acoustic comfort

findings.antecedent: Open plan environments with sufficient daylighting
findings.consequent: Productive workspaces (if acoustic design is not ignored)
findings.quote: Open plan environments with sufficient daylighting could be really productive workspaces as long as acoustic design is not ignored.

findings.antecedent: Square layout
findings.quote: If the area is square then the acoustic comfort is higher. However, when one has a long and narrow kind of space then acoustically one creates a bowling alley kind of effect where sound bounces between the two walls creating noise for the occupants

findings.antecedent: Under-floor heating (leads to elimination of carpets)
findings.quote: Use of under-floor heating leads to elimination of carpets which tend to absorb the sound

findings.antecedent: Harder material for floor and walls
findings.consequent: Noise in interior space (less sound absorption)
findings.quote: The harder the material, the lesser is its capability to absorb noise. Therefore, use of harder material results in more noise in the interior space

findings.antecedent: Green building parameters and practices
findings.quote: All these issues will eventually have an impact on occupant health and well-being. The examples above have demonstrated that it is possible that green building parameters and practices will have an impact on occupant health and well-being.

findings.antecedent: Passive design
findings.quote: The concept of passive design does attempt to combine thermal comfort and sustainable design

findings.antecedent: Providing control to occupants, training, and awareness
findings.consequent: Overall satisfaction of occupant from the building
findings.quote: Several strategies such as providing control to the occupants and providing them training and raise their awareness has an impact on the overall satisfaction of occupant from the building.

findings.antecedent: Urban areas (natural ventilation at night)
findings.consequent: Noise and pollution (due to lower traffic/outdoor activities)
findings.quote: Buildings in urban areas can have a higher level of natural ventilation at night as there is lower noise and pollution at night due to lower traffic and other outdoor activities around buildings.

findings.antecedent: IEQs considered throughout the lifecycle of the building (design, construction, commissioning, maintenance)
findings.quote: IEQs have to be considered throughout the lifecycle of the building. Decisions made at design, construction, commissioning and maintenance stages have an impact throughout the lifecycle of the building.

findings.antecedent: Design of exterior entrances with permanent entryways
findings.consequent: Dirt particles appearing in indoor space
findings.quote: Design of exterior entrances with permanent entryways captures dirt particles and avoids them from appearing in the indoor space.

findings.antecedent: Collaborative work with mechanical engineer
findings.consequent: Balance between energy efficiency and optimal fresh air
findings.quote: Collaborative work with the mechanical engineer can create a balance between energy efficiency and optimal amount of fresh air.

findings.antecedent: Source control (during operation of building)
findings.quote: Adequate IEQ is easiest to achieve when source control is practiced during the operation of each building since the indoor conditions or even the neighbourhood conditions may change frequently

findings.antecedent: Material selection (in a building)
findings.consequent: Building performance (thermal, indoor pollution, visual, acoustic comfort)
findings.quote: Materials have a crucial role to play on building performance and their selection requires special attention. Materials used in a building affect thermal performance, indoor pollution, visual comfort and acoustical comfort.

findings.antecedent: Architects and designers selecting materials that do not produce irritating odour or VOCs
findings.quote: Architects and designers can select materials that do not produce irritating odour or VOCs.

findings.antecedent: Choice of material
findings.quote: Choice of material can also help maximise sound absorbing ability.

findings.antecedent: Good sound masking system
findings.quote: good sound masking system can totally eliminate other acoustic problems post-occupancy.

findings.antecedent: Views and interaction of occupants with their natural environment
findings.quote: Design of buildings may also benefit from views and interaction of occupants with their natural environment.

findings.antecedent: Natural lighting and shading devices (to reduce direct glare)
findings.quote: It is beneficial to use natural lighting and at the same time use shading devices to reduce direct glare in the field of view.

findings.antecedent: Light colours in walls
findings.quote: The use of light colours in walls may also improve visual comfort.

findings.antecedent: Occupant control of lighting (dimming controls)
findings.quote: if occupants could be given control of lighting through dimming controls then it might further help achieve visual comfort

findings.antecedent: Monitoring and control (to ensure buildings deliver design intent)
findings.quote: there is a higher level of emphasis on monitoring and control to ensure that buildings are delivering what they are designed for

findings.antecedent: Building design incorporating occupant needs, comfort, and well-being
findings.quote: The principles of building design now need to incorporate occupant needs, comfort and well-being

synthesis_conclusions: The relationship between IEQ and occupant well-being and comfort, as well as the relationships among different IEQs, is complex.
Given that people spend over 90% of their lives indoors, understanding and acting on IEQ's impact is crucial.
Designers and engineers must consider sick building syndrome, thermal, visual, and acoustic comfort from the outset of building design.
Green building designs do not automatically guarantee occupant comfort and well-being; more specific and in-depth considerations are needed, balancing efficiency and sustainability.
Monitoring building and occupant performance during operations is essential, not just designing for potential comfort.
evidence_gaps: Further research is needed to evaluate different available approaches and standard questionnaires for occupants regarding IAQ.
More research is needed on the use of natural ventilation in cities with high outdoor air pollution.
Acoustic comfort is still lacking despite existing knowledge and green building guidelines.
More research is needed to make acoustic comfort a mandatory element of green building guidelines.
More research is needed to study daylight, artificial lighting, glare, and visual comfort holistically.
Future research can concentrate on IEQ's relation to occupant productivity, behavior, and behavior change.
Future research can develop state-of-the-art studies on IEQ's impact on health and well-being in school, retail, and residential buildings.
Future research can connect findings to various green building rating systems (LEED, BREEAM, GSAS).
limitations: The study limited its focus on occupant's health and well-being, not productivity or behavior.
The study limited its focus on office buildings.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Occupants adapt to their indoor thermal environment, and their comfort expectations are influenced by outdoor climate and personal factors.
Excessive or inappropriate environmental stimuli (e.g., noise, poor air quality) can lead to cognitive overload and stress, negatively impacting well-being.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper reviews various causal pathways through which specific indoor environmental quality (IEQ) factors influence occupant well-being and comfort. A common pathway involves physiological and psychological responses to environmental stimuli.

steps.from_construct: Poor indoor air quality (e.g., high CO2, VOCs)
